overview: Whether a virus steals a lipid membrane on its way out of the cell decides how fragile it is and what kills it.

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: Viruses surrounded by a lipid bilayer envelope, typically acquired from host cell membranes during budding.
aspects.valueB: Viruses whose outermost layer is a protein capsid only, with no lipid membrane.

aspects.label: Environmental Stability
aspects.valueA: Generally fragile — sensitive to drying, heat, detergents, and alcohol.
aspects.valueB: Generally hardier — can survive on surfaces, in water, and resist many disinfectants for longer.

aspects.label: Disinfectant Susceptibility
aspects.valueA: Easily inactivated by soap, alcohol-based hand rubs, and most standard disinfectants.
aspects.valueB: Often resistant to alcohol and requires stronger measures (e.g. bleach) for reliable inactivation.

aspects.label: Typical Transmission Route
aspects.valueA: Often via respiratory droplets, blood, sexual contact, or requires direct contact due to fragility.
aspects.valueB: Often via the fecal-oral route or fomites, since they survive well outside the host.

aspects.label: Cell Entry Mechanism
aspects.valueA: Membrane fusion between the viral envelope and host cell membrane.
aspects.valueB: Receptor-mediated endocytosis or direct capsid penetration.

aspects.label: Key Distinguishing Feature
aspects.valueA: Has a lipid envelope, fragile outside the host.
aspects.valueB: No lipid envelope, more environmentally resistant.

overlay.examHighYieldNote: If alcohol-based sanitizer 'doesn't work well' against a virus, suspect it's non-enveloped (e.g. norovirus).
